It's February. Andrei is taking the Goethe A2 exam on Monday, so that he can do a master's in Berlin in the autumn. It's Sunday evening and Mara is testing him in the kitchen, with a pile of flashcards.
Right, last round. I say a sentence, you correct it. “Gestern ich bin ins Kino gegangen.”
Wrong. The verb has to be in second position. “Gestern bin ich ins Kino gegangen.”
Good. “Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich bin krank.”
After “weil” the verb goes to the end. “…, weil ich krank bin.” That's easy.
And now the cases. “Ich fahre mit die Straßenbahn zu der Arbeit.”
“Mit” and “zu” take the dative. “Ich fahre mit der Straßenbahn zur Arbeit.” Zur, not zu der.
Perfect. Last question, the hardest one: “Ich habe gestern nach Potsdam gefahren.”
Ha! The trap! “Fahren” is movement, so it takes “sein”: “Ich bin gestern nach Potsdam gefahren.” Ludwig has told me that a hundred times.
You're ready, Andrei. Honestly. If you play like you did today, you'll pass.
And the speaking test? What happens if I get nervous and forget everything?
Then you take a deep breath and think of Lena. You've spoken German with her every evening, for months. The speaking test is your best part.
And what do I do tomorrow morning, before the exam?
Sleep well, have a good breakfast and pop in briefly to see Mrs Hoffmann. She said she wants to tell you something. She's on my ward, room twelve.
“LOONG-en-ent-TSÜN-doong”: a long word; split it up: Lungen + Entzündung.

The verbal bracket: the second part of the verb (past participle, infinitive, separable prefix) goes to the end of the main clause:
Perfekt: the past participle at the end.
Modal: the infinitive at the end.
Separable: the prefix at the end.
Passive: the past participle at the end.
direct object; durch, für, gegen, ohne, um; wohin?
indirect object; aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu; wo?; helfen, danken, gefallen
The nine two-way prepositions (in, an, auf, unter, über, vor, hinter, neben, zwischen): Wohin? → Akkusativ, Wo? → Dativ.

At the beginning of February, Mrs Hoffmann had fallen ill. At first it was just a cough, then came the fever, and after three days she could hardly breathe. Ludwig found her one Wednesday morning, when she didn't open the door to him, and called an ambulance. The diagnosis was pneumonia. At ninety-two, that's dangerous. She was taken to ward 4, Mara's ward, to room twelve, the same room where, more than two years earlier, Mr Schulz had lain, the man who spoke only Berlin dialect.

The first days were hard. Every morning Mara came an hour before her shift to sit with her, and every evening she stayed longer. Dr Yılmaz looked after her personally. Ludwig came every afternoon on the M1, with flowers, with newspapers that he read to her and with Fritz, whom he hid in a big bag, because dogs weren't allowed in the hospital. Everyone knew. Nobody said anything.

After a week she was better. The fever went down, she could sit up again, and on the eighth day she complained about the food for the first time. “That's a good sign,” Dr Yılmaz told Mara. “When patients complain about the food, they're getting better.”

The night before Andrei's exam, Mara was on the night shift. At two o'clock she saw a light in room twelve. Mrs Hoffmann was lying awake, moving her fingers on the blanket as if she were playing the piano. “I'm practising,” she said when Mara came in. “Without a piano. In my head. I learnt that in the war, in the cellar, when we weren't allowed to play.” Mara sat down beside her, and for half an hour they watched together as the old fingers danced on the blanket, Chopin, without a single note.

On Monday morning, at seven, Andrei knocked on the door of room twelve. He was nervous, not because of Mrs Hoffmann, but because of the exam, which started at nine at the Goethe-Institut. He had hardly slept. He had drunk three coffees. In his bag he had two pencils, a rubber, his passport and a piece of plum cake from Lena, “for the nerves”.

Mrs Hoffmann was sitting in bed, pale but with bright eyes, and on her knees lay the grey blanket Mara had given her for her birthday. She looked at him and smiled. “Sit down, lad,” she said. “I haven't got much time, the nurse is coming with the pills in a minute. And you haven't got much time either.”

I've taken hundreds of exams in my life. Concerts, competitions, recordings. And I've learnt this: examiners don't want to see that you're perfect. They want to see that you're playing. That you're alive. If you make a mistake, keep playing. Do you understand?
I understand. Keep playing. Like at the fifth note.

Mrs Hoffmann laughed, and then she had to cough. When she had calmed down, she took his hand in both her thin hands. “And one more thing. If you don't know what to say in the speaking test, talk about something you love. Then you'll find the words. The words always come when you love something.”

The exam lasted the whole morning. The reading was easy: an email about a birthday party, a notice in a supermarket, a short article about bees in the city. Andrei almost laughed. The listening was harder. In an announcement at the station he only understood “line” and “delay”, but that was enough. In the writing he had to write an email to a friend and invite him to a party. He wrote about a courtyard party with fairy lights and music from the fourth floor.

In the afternoon came the speaking test. The examiner was an older gentleman with a friendly beard. The first task was simple: introduce yourself. Andrei gave his name, his age, where he was from. Then the examiner asked: “And what do you like doing in your free time?” Andrei opened his mouth. And suddenly everything had gone. Every word, every rule. His head was empty. All he could hear was his heart beating.

Then he thought of Mrs Hoffmann in her bed, of her thin hands, of her voice: talk about something you love. He took a deep breath. And then he talked. About a bakery on Kastanienallee, where he shaped pretzels every morning at four. About a baker who had laughed at his first pretzels, because they looked like snakes. About an old tram driver who showed him Berlin, house by house, story by story. About a brown notebook in which he wrote everything down. He talked for five minutes, without a break, with mistakes, with a Romanian accent, but he talked.

When he had finished, the examiner looked at him for a long time. Then he put down his pen and said, not as an examiner but as a person: “You know, young man, I've been doing this job for twenty years. And that was the most beautiful answer to the free-time question I've ever heard.”

In the evening, Andrei went straight to the hospital, to room twelve. Lena was already there, and Ludwig, and Mara in her white uniform, and Fritz in the big bag. Mrs Hoffmann looked at Andrei and asked only: “Well? Did you keep playing?” Andrei nodded. “I talked about something I love,” he said, and looked at Lena. “The words came.” Mrs Hoffmann smiled and closed her eyes. “You see,” she said quietly. “That's the whole secret. In music and in life.”

Three weeks later the result came by email. Andrei had passed, with ninety-three points out of a hundred. In the speaking he had the top score. He read the email at four in the morning, in the bakery, with flour on his hands, and Lena read it over his shoulder. Then Lena printed out the email and hung it on the wall next to the till, beside the old photo of Grandma Ingrid, so that every customer could see it. And Mrs Hoffmann, who had come home a week earlier, played a particularly cheerful piece at nine that evening. For the candidate from Sibiu.
Downstairs, on the first floor, Ludwig opened the window, so that he could hear every note.
Was sagte Frau Hoffmann zu Andrei?
Er soll von etwas erzählen, das er liebt.
Er soll nicht zur Prüfung gehen.
von der Bäckerei, Lena und Ludwig
